title: Design Uber (Ride Matching)
summary: End-to-end walkthrough: absorb a million location pings per second in an in-memory geo index, match without double-assigning drivers, and keep trip state durable.
body:
## Practice first

Design a ride-hailing service. A rider enters a pickup and destination, sees a fare estimate, and requests a ride. Nearby drivers are offered the trip; one accepts, drives to the rider, and completes the trip.

Spend about 10 minutes sketching before you read on: requirements, entities, the rider and driver endpoints, a baseline, and the two hardest problems you would deep-dive. Then compare.

## Functional requirements

Core (users should be able to):

1. **Riders request a ride** from a pickup to a destination after seeing a fare estimate.
2. **Drivers share their location and availability**, and accept or decline ride offers.
3. **The system matches** each request to a nearby available driver, and both parties track the trip through pickup and drop-off.

Out of scope: surge pricing, ratings, payments processing (assume a payment service is called at trip end), scheduled rides, pooling multiple riders, and detailed ETA/routing algorithms (we call a routing service as a black box).

## Non-functional requirements

- **Matching latency:** a rider should be matched (or told nobody is available) within ~1 minute; the first offer should reach a driver within a couple of seconds.
- **Consistency of assignment:** a driver must never be assigned two rides at once, and a ride must never have two drivers. This is strongly consistent per driver and per ride; we accept occasionally re-offering a ride over ever double-assigning.
- **Location freshness and throughput:** driver positions should be at most a few seconds stale for matching; the system must absorb a very high, steady write rate of location pings.
- **Availability:** requesting and matching should be highly available (99.99%) and partitioned by city so one region's failure does not take down others.
- **Durability of trips:** once a trip is accepted, its state (and later its completion and fare) must survive server crashes; location pings, by contrast, are disposable.

## Back-of-the-envelope

- **Location writes:** assume 5M drivers online at global peak, each sending a ping every 4 s: 5M / 4 ≈ **1.25M writes/s**. Each ping is tiny (~100 bytes) and superseded 4 s later. Decision: **do not write pings to a disk-backed transactional database**; keep the latest position in an in-memory geospatial index, and stream raw pings to a log only if analytics needs them.
- **Ride requests:** say 30M trips/day ≈ 350/s average, perhaps 2,000/s peak. Matching and trip writes are modest; a sharded relational store handles them. Decision: **the hard part is contention and correctness, not trip throughput.**
- **Proximity query cost:** a city with 50,000 online drivers queried by brute-force distance on every request costs 50,000 distance computations per request; at 100 requests/s per big city that is 5M/s per city. Decision: **index drivers spatially (geohash or H3 cells)** so a query touches a few cells with tens to hundreds of drivers.
- **Memory:** 5M drivers × ~200 bytes (id, lat/lng, status, cell, timestamp) ≈ 1 GB. The whole live index fits in memory many times over; sharding is for write throughput and fault isolation, not capacity.

## Core entities

- **Rider** and **Driver:** identities; the driver also has a vehicle and current status (`offline`, `available`, `offered`, `on_trip`).
- **DriverLocation:** driver id, lat/lng, heading, timestamp; ephemeral, latest-only.
- **Ride (trip):** id, rider, driver (nullable), pickup, destination, fare estimate, state, version.
- **Offer:** ride id, driver id, expires at, outcome.

The trip is a state machine:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Requested
    Requested --> Matching
    Matching --> DriverAssigned: driver accepts
    Matching --> NoDrivers: timeout
    DriverAssigned --> DriverArrived
    DriverArrived --> InProgress: rider picked up
    InProgress --> Completed
    DriverAssigned --> Cancelled
    Matching --> Cancelled
    Completed --> [*]
    Cancelled --> [*]
    NoDrivers --> [*]
```

Every transition is a conditional write on the ride row (`WHERE state = :expected`), which makes duplicate or out-of-order client events harmless.

## API

```http
POST /v1/fares/estimate
Authorization: Bearer <rider token>
{ "pickup": { "lat": 37.776, "lng": -122.417 }, "destination": { "lat": 37.615, "lng": -122.390 } }
200 OK { "estimateId": "est_5", "fare": { "amount": 4250, "currency": "USD" }, "etaSeconds": 240, "expiresAt": "..." }

POST /v1/rides
Authorization: Bearer <rider token>
Idempotency-Key: 9b2c...
{ "estimateId": "est_5" }
201 Created { "rideId": "r_19", "state": "matching" }
```

```http
POST /v1/drivers/me/location
Authorization: Bearer <driver token>
{ "lat": 37.7751, "lng": -122.4183, "heading": 90, "ts": 1793228470 }
204 No Content

PATCH /v1/rides/{rideId}/offer
Authorization: Bearer <driver token>
{ "decision": "accept" }
200 OK { "rideId": "r_19", "state": "driver_assigned" }
409 Conflict { "reason": "offer expired or ride already taken" }

PATCH /v1/rides/{rideId}
{ "state": "in_progress", "expectedState": "driver_arrived" }
```

Riders and drivers use different token scopes; driver identity is never taken from the body. The fare estimate is signed or stored server-side so a client cannot edit the price. Offers and trip updates are delivered to apps via a persistent push channel (WebSocket or mobile push), with polling as a fallback.

## High-level design

**Requirement 1, request.** The Ride service validates the estimate, creates a ride in `requested`, and hands it to the Matching service. The rider app subscribes to updates for that ride.

**Requirement 2, driver location.** Driver apps send pings to a Location service, which updates an in-memory geospatial index (Redis `GEO` commands or a custom service keyed by H3 cell), partitioned by city or region. Each entry has a short TTL so drivers who stop pinging fall out of the index automatically.

**Requirement 3, match and track.** The Matching service queries the index for available drivers near the pickup, ranks them (straight-line distance first, then ETA from the routing service for the top few), and offers the ride to one driver at a time with a short timeout. Acceptance runs a conditional update that assigns driver and ride atomically. During the trip, the driver's location stream is forwarded to the rider.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R["Rider app"] --> GW["API gateway"]
    D["Driver app"] --> GW
    GW --> RS["Ride service"]
    GW --> LS["Location service"]
    LS --> GEO[("In-memory geo index, per city")]
    RS --> RDB[("Rides DB, sharded by city")]
    RS --> MS["Matching service"]
    MS --> GEO
    MS --> ETA["Routing and ETA service"]
    MS --> LOCK[("Driver lock store")]
    MS --> PUSH["Push gateway (WebSocket)"]
    PUSH --> D
    PUSH --> R
```

Walk a request: the rider requests from Mission District; the Ride service writes `r_19` and calls Matching. Matching asks the geo index for available drivers within 2 km, gets 40 candidates, asks the ETA service for the best 10, and picks driver `d_7`. It atomically reserves `d_7` with a 15-second lock and sends an offer through the push gateway. The driver taps accept; the Ride service conditionally sets `r_19` to `driver_assigned` with `driver_id = d_7`, and the driver's status becomes `on_trip`. The rider's app starts receiving `d_7`'s location.

## Deep dives

### 1. Ingesting 1.25 million location updates per second (write throughput)

**Bad: write every ping to the primary relational database and query with a lat/lng range.** Over a million durable writes per second plus a two-dimensional range scan on a B-tree is expensive, and the data is obsolete 4 seconds later.

**Good: a database with a geospatial index (PostGIS, or a geo-indexed document store).** Proximity queries become efficient, but the store is still paying for durability, replication and index maintenance on data that has a 4-second shelf life.

**Great: an in-memory geo index partitioned by region.** Encode each position into a cell (geohash or H3). Store `driver → (cell, lat, lng, ts, status)` and `cell → set of drivers` in memory: Redis `GEOADD`/`GEOSEARCH` (a geohash-scored sorted set) or a purpose-built service. Partition by city so each shard handles one metro's writes and queries, and replicate for failover. Losing a node only loses a few seconds of positions; drivers re-ping and repopulate it, so no durable write is needed. Clients can adapt ping frequency: every 4 s when available, less often when stationary, more often during pickup.

The cell size matters: too large and each query returns thousands of drivers; too small and a 2 km radius covers hundreds of cells. Query the pickup cell plus its neighbours (a geohash cell can put a nearby driver just across a boundary) and expand rings if too few drivers are found.

### 2. One driver, one ride (consistency under concurrency)

Two matching workers handling two nearby riders can both pick the same closest driver. If both send offers and the driver accepts the first, the second rider waits for a ride that will never come; worse, a naïve implementation assigns the driver to both.

**Bad: check driver status, then send the offer.** A read-check-write race between workers.

**Good: a conditional update on the driver's status in the database.** `UPDATE drivers SET status = 'offered', offer_ride = :r, offer_expires = now() + 15s WHERE id = :d AND (status = 'available' OR (status = 'offered' AND offer_expires < now()))`. Only one worker gets one row back. Correct, but it puts the hot driver-status path on the transactional database.

**Great: a short-lived lease in a fast, consistent store, with the authoritative assignment in the ride database.** Reserve the driver with `SET driver_lock:d_7 r_19 NX PX 15000` in Redis (or a compare-and-set in a strongly consistent key-value store). The winner sends the offer. On accept, one transaction (or two conditional writes in a fixed order) sets the ride to `driver_assigned` with `WHERE state = 'matching'` and the driver to `on_trip` with `WHERE status IN ('available','offered') AND offer_ride = :r`. The lease only prevents duplicate offers; the conditional writes are what guarantee correctness, so a lease that expires early (GC pause, clock issues) can cause a wasted offer but never a double assignment. On decline or timeout, the lease is deleted or expires and the next candidate is tried.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant M1 as Matcher (ride r_19)
    participant M2 as Matcher (ride r_20)
    participant L as Lock store
    participant P as Push gateway
    participant D as Driver d_7
    participant DB as Rides DB
    M1->>L: SET lock d_7 = r_19 NX, 15 s
    L-->>M1: OK
    M2->>L: SET lock d_7 = r_20 NX, 15 s
    L-->>M2: exists
    M2->>M2: try next driver
    M1->>P: offer r_19 to d_7
    P->>D: offer (expires in 15 s)
    D->>DB: accept r_19
    DB->>DB: conditional update ride and driver
    DB-->>D: assigned
```

The lock store stops the second matcher from offering the same driver; the database's conditional update is the final word on assignment. If the driver accepts after the lease expired and the ride was re-offered and taken, the conditional update fails and the driver gets a 409.

### 3. Matching loop and timeouts (latency)

Matching is a short-lived workflow per ride: find candidates, offer to one, wait up to ~15 s, move on. If the Matching worker crashes mid-loop, the ride sits in `matching` forever. Run it as a durable workflow: put ride requests on a queue partitioned by city; workers process them and checkpoint progress (candidates tried) on the ride row or in a workflow engine. A timer or delayed message re-drives any ride that has been in `matching` longer than expected. Offering to one driver at a time is fair and avoids wasted driver attention; offering to two or three in parallel lowers latency in sparse areas at the cost of more declines. After ~60 s without acceptance, transition to `no_drivers` and notify the rider.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q[["Ride requests, partitioned by city"]] --> W["Matching worker"]
    W --> C["Query nearby available drivers"]
    C --> E["Rank by ETA"]
    E --> L["Lease top driver"]
    L --> O["Send offer, wait 15 s"]
    O -->|"accepted"| A["Assign: conditional writes"]
    O -->|"declined or timeout"| N{"Time left and candidates?"}
    N -->|"yes"| L
    N -->|"no"| X["Mark no drivers, notify rider"]
```

The loop is bounded by both a candidate list and a total deadline. Because each step is idempotent (leases and conditional writes), a crashed worker's ride can simply be re-driven by another worker.

### 4. ETA, briefly (accuracy vs cost)

Straight-line distance is a poor proxy in cities with rivers, one-way streets and traffic. But calling a routing engine for 50 candidates per request is expensive. Use a two-stage ranking: filter by straight-line distance from the geo index, then ask the routing service (road graph with live traffic, often with precomputed contraction hierarchies) for ETAs to the top 5–10. Cache recent ETAs between cell pairs for a few seconds.

### 5. Durable trip state and failure handling (durability and availability)

The ride row is the source of truth for everything that matters financially: who drove, when pickup and drop-off happened, the agreed fare. Store rides in a replicated relational or distributed SQL database, sharded by city (most queries are local; cross-city trips are rare and still have a home shard). Every transition is a conditional update with the expected state, and client calls carry idempotency keys, so retries from flaky mobile networks cannot advance a trip twice. Driver apps buffer state changes made while offline (for example "trip completed" in a tunnel) and replay them with original timestamps. Location data during the trip is sampled to durable storage (every few seconds) for fare computation and disputes, separate from the ephemeral geo index. If the geo index for a city fails over, matching degrades for a few seconds until drivers re-ping, but existing trips are unaffected because they live in the ride database.

## What interviewers look for

- **Mid-level:** a working request → match → trip flow, a separate path for location updates, and some spatial index instead of scanning all drivers.
- **Senior:** quantifies the location write rate and justifies in-memory, TTL'd geo storage; prevents double assignment with leases plus conditional updates; designs offer timeouts; models the trip as a durable state machine.
- **Staff:** partitions by city for fault isolation and explains cross-boundary behaviour, treats matching as a durable workflow with re-drive, reasons about lease expiry versus correctness (why the database write is the fencing step), adaptive ping rates for battery and cost, and degradation modes during regional failures.

## Common mistakes

- Storing every location ping durably in the main database.
- Querying "drivers within 2 km" with `lat BETWEEN ... AND lng BETWEEN ...` on two separate indexes.
- Ignoring cell boundaries, so nearby drivers in the neighbouring cell are missed.
- Relying solely on a distributed lock for correctness, with no conditional write behind it.
- Holding a ride in `matching` with no timeout or re-drive when a worker dies.
- Pulling surge pricing or detailed routing into scope and running out of time for matching.

## Self-review checklist

- [ ] Location updates are sized (writes/s) and stored in a way that matches their shelf life.
- [ ] Proximity search touches a bounded number of cells, including neighbours.
- [ ] A driver can be offered only one ride at a time, and assignment is a conditional write.
- [ ] Offers time out and the matching loop survives worker crashes.
- [ ] Trip states and transitions are explicit and idempotent.
- [ ] Partitioning by city is justified and its edge cases named.
- [ ] Out-of-scope features stayed out of scope.

## Further reading

- [H3: hexagonal hierarchical geospatial indexing system](https://h3geo.org/docs/)
- [Redis: Geospatial indexes](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/geospatial/)

keyTakeaways: Driver pings are high-volume and disposable: keep the latest position in an in-memory, TTL'd geospatial index partitioned by city.
Proximity search should touch a bounded set of geohash or H3 cells, including neighbours, then rank a short list by real ETA.
A short lease prevents offering one driver two rides; a conditional write on ride and driver is what actually guarantees one-driver-one-ride.
Matching is a durable, timed workflow with offer timeouts and re-drive, so a crashed worker never strands a ride.
The trip is an explicit state machine persisted with conditional, idempotent transitions, separate from ephemeral location data.
